summary: This informational document describes the applicability of the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) through use case studies and network design considerations. The use cases include Metro Ethernet access and aggregation transport, mobile backhaul, and packet optical transport.

eli5.summary: This shows real jobs where a certain kind of network technology fits, such as city networks and phone towers.

questions: where is mpls transport profile applied
when to use mpls-tp vs ip mpls
subtitle: Real-world applications of MPLS-TP in modern packet transport networks.

tldr.problem: Service providers are transitioning from aging TDM and ATM technologies to packet-based networks, but traditional IP/MPLS is designed for service delivery, not core transport operations.
tldr.mechanism: MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is a streamlined subset of MPLS functions optimized for carrier-grade transport: it supports static provisioning, advanced fault detection and recovery, and operations expertise familiar to transport engineers.
tldr.outcome: Service providers can replace legacy transport infrastructure with unified MPLS technology throughout their networks (core, aggregation, access), reducing operational complexity and cost while supporting multiple services.

facts.label: Key features
facts.value: Bidirectional LSPs, BFD probes, fast protection

today: RFC 6965 is Informational. MPLS-TP is deployed by major service providers in metro access, mobile backhaul, and packet optical networks as of 2013. It is not obsoleted; it represents an important architectural approach for carriers managing the transition from circuit-based to packet-based transport.

sections.title: Transport Networks and MPLS-TP
sections.content:
Service providers operate transport networks that move data across cities, regions, and continents. Historically, these networks used circuit-based technologies like SONET/SDH (Synchronous Optical Network) and ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode). These technologies reserved fixed bandwidth per connection and offered excellent reliability, but they were expensive to maintain and wasted bandwidth during quiet periods.

Packet-based transport is more efficient: it uses statistical multiplexing to share bandwidth among many connections, achieving better utilization. However, IP/MPLS (the dominant packet technology) was designed primarily for service features like VPNs and video delivery. MPLS-TP takes the core packet-forwarding mechanisms of MPLS and streamlines them for transport operations, adding specialized tools for fault management, protection, and provisioning that carriers need.
sections.eli5: Old transport systems reserved a fixed lane for each customer, even if they weren't using it. Packet systems share lanes efficiently. MPLS-TP is packet forwarding tuned for how carriers (not just ISPs) actually manage networks.

sections.title: Three Major Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC details three primary scenarios where MPLS-TP fits well. Metro access and aggregation involves connecting customers and branch offices to regional data centers. Service providers are replacing ATM or TDM aggregation layers with MPLS-TP, achieving higher efficiency and supporting flexible bandwidth allocation. The Unified MPLS strategy uses MPLS-TP in these layers, MPLS in the core, creating a single technology from access to backbone.

Packet optical transport addresses networks where both packet and optical layers exist. MPLS-TP allows operators to manage traffic as virtual circuits (called LSPs or Label Switched Paths) that can be either statically provisioned or dynamically controlled. Both packet and optical networks can use the same management model.

Mobile backhaul connects base stations to controllers. In 2G/3G networks, this is a hub-and-spoke star topology; MPLS-TP's bidirectional LSPs and static provisioning match this perfectly. In 4G/LTE, the topology is more mesh-like; MPLS-TP supports both static provisioning for simplicity or dynamic control plane for optimization.
sections.eli5: MPLS-TP works well for connecting branch offices (metro access), for networks mixing packet and fiber (optical transport), and for mobile towers connecting back to the company network (mobile backhaul).

sections.title: Provisioning and Design Decisions
sections.content:
MPLS-TP supports two provisioning modes. Static provisioning means an operator manually configures each circuit through a network management system (NMS), just like traditional transport. This appeals to carriers with strong transport expertise. Dynamic control plane allows routers to automatically set up and adapt circuits, useful for flexible service provisioning. Operators can blend both modes—some circuits static, others dynamic—during transition periods.

Key design choices include whether to use SS-PW (single-segment pseudowire, simpler) or MS-PW (multi-segment pseudowire, more complex but with domain isolation), whether to layer protection at the LSP level, the PW level, or both, and how to tune fault detection intervals. Faster detection (shorter BFD probe intervals) finds failures quicker but uses more processing power. The RFC emphasizes that simpler designs often win: operational simplicity sometimes outweighs theoretical optimization.
sections.eli5: Carriers can configure circuits by hand (static, familiar to transport teams) or let routers auto-configure (dynamic, more flexible). They choose between simple single-path circuits or complex multi-segment ones. They balance fast failure detection against CPU cost.

sections.title: Operations, Administration, and Maintenance
sections.content:
MPLS-TP provides a rich toolkit for managing networks. OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) tools include proactive mechanisms (like BFD continuity checks sent regularly) that detect failures before customers notice, and on-demand mechanisms (like Link Down Indication) triggered by actual faults. When a fiber is cut, special ICMP-like messages (LSP Ping) trace the issue; when a link fails, Link Down Indication signals immediate switchover.

Protection mechanisms let traffic automatically switch from a failed path to a backup path. Ring protection works for ring-shaped topologies; linear protection for point-to-point links; shared mesh protection for complex topologies. Choosing the right protection strategy affects both recovery time and resource usage.
sections.eli5: MPLS-TP watches the network continuously (proactive OAM) and responds instantly when problems occur. When a link fails, traffic switches to a backup path automatically. Different network shapes (rings, lines, meshes) use different protection strategies.

sections.title: Standards Compliance and Future Evolution
sections.content:
MPLS-TP is a joint work between the IETF and ITU-T, giving it strong standards foundation. The ITU-T specified the transport requirements; the IETF developed the protocols. This alignment benefits carriers globally, ensuring multi-vendor interoperability and industry confidence.

One challenge: service providers' core networks often still run legacy MPLS/IP. Full end-to-end MPLS-TP OAM cannot traverse legacy cores today. The interim approach is to tunnel MPLS-TP LSPs over the legacy IP/MPLS network, running legacy OAM on the tunnel. Over time, as core routers upgrade to support MPLS-TP features, this limitation disappears. The RFC acknowledges that MPLS-TP is not designed to replace IP/MPLS service features (like L3VPN or IPTV); rather, it complements them.
sections.eli5: MPLS-TP is standardized by both IETF and ITU-T, helping different vendors work together. Old networks still use older MPLS; new MPLS-TP networks can work with them by tunneling through. Eventually everything will upgrade.
